(CNN) -- Children from a polygamist sect who one mother says are "hurting very badly" in state custody are likely to be returned to their parents, a CNN legal analyst says. FLDS member Margaret Jessop says her children "feel betrayed by adults." A Texas appeals court ruled Thursday that the state had no right to remove hundreds of children from the Fundamentalist Church of Latter-Day Saints' ranch in Eldorado on April 3, based on the suspicion that a few were being sexually abused. A sect mother who has four children in state custody said the matter has not been fully resolved because an appeal to the Texas Supreme Court is possible. "I'm very grateful, but I'd like to see the children in my arms before I rejoice greatly," Margaret Jessop said on CNN's "Larry King Live."  Watch Jessop react to the ruling » . But a permanent reunion of families is likely, said Jeffrey Toobin, CNN senior legal analyst. "Based on this ruling I think it's clear that if it stands, all these kids are going back with their mothers," Toobin said on CNN's "Anderson Cooper 360°." Jessop and other FLDS parents said they had been permitted visits with their children in foster care. Zavenda Young said two of her children were sent to Waco, Texas, and two to Hockley, 148 miles away. "They're in Boys and Girls Country in Hockley. And it's just a -- it's an institution," she told host Larry King. Their father, Edson Jessop, said the experience has been rough on the children. "You can see it's a lot of stress on them," he said. "Every time we leave, they go through that trauma again. It's enough to rip your heart out." "They feel betrayed by adults, and they're hurting very badly," Margaret Jessop added. The Texas Child Protective Services Department's Web site says the agency has been "coordinating with many professional service and government agencies to ensure the safety, health and comfort of the children and women in Eldorado." A statement from the agency Thursday said it's working out a response to the court ruling. "Child Protective Services has one duty -- to protect children," the statement said. "When we see evidence that children have been sexually abused and remain at risk of further abuse, we will act. ... We will work with the office of the attorney general to determine the state's next step in this case."

**Texas appeals court: FLDS children likely to be returned to parents**

**AUSTIN, Texas** — Hundreds of children taken from a polygamist sect’s ranch in West Texas are likely to be returned to their parents after a state appeals court ruled that Texas child welfare officials failed to justify keeping them in foster care.

The 3rd Court of Appeals in Austin ruled Thursday that a lower court abused its discretion when it ordered the children from the Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints compound near Eldorado to remain in state custody. The court said Texas officials did not present enough evidence that all of the children were in immediate danger.

The ruling marked a major setback for Child Protective Services, which removed more than 400 children from the Yearning for Zion Ranch in April after authorities said they received a call alleging abuse. The raid led to one of the largest child-custody actions in U.S. history.

Parents from the FLDS community welcomed the decision.

“I’m very, very happy,” Margaret Jessop, an FLDS mother, said after the ruling. “I just want my children back.”

CNN legal analyst Jeffrey Toobin described the decision as a significant rebuke of the state’s handling of the case.

“This is a stinging defeat for Texas authorities,” Toobin said, noting that the court rejected the state’s argument that the entire community of children could be treated as endangered based on allegations involving some underage girls.

Child Protective Services said it was reviewing the ruling and considering its legal options.

“Our priority has always been the safety and well-being of the children,” the agency said in a statement. “We are disappointed in the court’s decision and will continue to work to protect children who may be at risk.”

The appeals court did not immediately order every child returned, but its decision directed the trial court to vacate the custody order that kept the children in foster care. Attorneys for the parents said that means reunifications could begin soon unless the state obtains emergency relief from the Texas Supreme Court.

State officials had argued that girls at the ranch were being groomed for underage marriages and that boys were being raised in an environment that encouraged abuse. Lawyers for the parents countered that the state had failed to show specific evidence of abuse or imminent danger for each child.

The appeals court sided with the parents on that point, saying the state could not remove all children from the ranch solely because some adults may have engaged in illegal conduct.

The FLDS church, a breakaway sect not affiliated with the mainstream Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, has long been under scrutiny over allegations of polygamy and underage marriage. Church members denied that the children at the Texas ranch were in danger.

The ruling leaves open the possibility that CPS could continue investigations involving individual children or families, but it sharply limits the sweeping custody action that began with the April raid.

**Court: Texas Had No Right to Remove Hundreds of FLDS Children From Ranch**

In a major rebuke to Texas child-welfare authorities, an appeals court ruled that the state had no legal basis to seize hundreds of children from a polygamist sect’s ranch, finding that officials failed to show the children faced an immediate danger requiring mass removal.

The decision centered on the April 2008 raid of the Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints’ Yearning for Zion Ranch near Eldorado, Texas. Acting after reports of sexual abuse and underage marriage, Texas authorities removed more than 400 children from the ranch and placed them in state custody.

But the court said the state’s action went too far. Judges concluded that Texas Child Protective Services had not presented evidence that every child taken from the ranch was at imminent risk of abuse. The ruling said the state could not treat the entire FLDS community as a single household or presume danger to all children based on allegations involving some families.

The case drew national attention and was heavily discussed on CNN programs including **“Larry King Live”** and **“Anderson Cooper 360°.”** In those interviews, FLDS representatives and attorneys argued that the state had punished an entire religious community without proving individual abuse. They insisted many of the children taken were infants and young boys who were not connected to allegations of forced underage marriage.

On **“Larry King Live,”** FLDS spokesman Willie Jessop and others defended the families, saying mothers and children had been traumatized by the separation and that the sect was being judged largely by suspicion and stereotype. Attorneys for the parents argued that the state’s evidence was too broad and that child-welfare law requires specific proof of danger to each child.

On **“Anderson Cooper 360°,”** CNN reported on the central legal question: whether allegations of a culture that tolerated underage marriage were enough to justify removing every child from the ranch. The program also examined the origins of the raid, including the phone calls that triggered the investigation. Authorities had said they were responding to a report from a girl claiming abuse at the ranch; later scrutiny raised questions about whether that call was authentic.

Texas officials maintained that they acted to protect children from a system they believed encouraged sexual abuse of minors. They pointed to evidence of underage pregnancies and marriages within the FLDS community, arguing that girls at the ranch were at risk in an environment controlled by adult men and religious leaders.

The court, however, said suspicion of a harmful culture was not enough. It ruled that the state had to demonstrate a continuing, immediate danger to the specific children it removed—and that it had failed to do so for the vast majority.

The decision opened the door for children to be returned to their parents, though it did not end the broader investigation into alleged abuse at the ranch. Texas authorities could still pursue individual cases where evidence supported intervention.

The ruling marked a turning point in one of the largest child-custody actions in American history, pitting religious freedom and parental rights against the state’s duty to protect children. For the FLDS families, it was a vindication of their argument that the raid was an unconstitutional overreach. For child-welfare officials, it was a setback in a case they had described as an urgent effort to protect vulnerable minors.
